```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This file sits between `01_join_and_clean.Rmd` and `02_analysis.Rmd`. It
describes the data before any model is fitted: what the variables look like,
what is missing, and what the patterns are.

Every visual below states the question it is there to answer. A chart that
does not answer a question does not belong in the paper.

**Loading everything.** I load the tidyverse for data handling and plotting, and
`patchwork`, which is used once at the very end to place two finished plots side
by side. The data comes from `data_clean/analysis_data.csv`, the single file
produced by `01_join_and_clean.Rmd`. Printing `dim()` is a habit: if this does
not say 89 rows and 13 columns, something upstream has changed and I should stop
and find out why before going any further.

```{r load}
# patchwork is only used for the final side-by-side figure.
# install.packages("patchwork")
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

data <- read_csv("data_clean/analysis_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(data)
```


# Part 1: Where the data comes from

All three sources were downloaded directly from the organisation that publishes
them, by `00_download_sources.R`, and joined on ISO-3 country code in
`01_join_and_clean.Rmd`. None came from a data aggregator or a pre-cleaned copy,
and nothing was edited by hand at any stage.

## Source 1 — Internet use by gender

**World Bank Global Findex Database 2025.** Gallup surveyed adults aged 15 and
over in each country between May and December 2024, asking the same internet-use
question everywhere.

- Landing page: <https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/globalfindex>
- File used: <https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/be6615202d1f08a25855c8ac2d615122-0050012025/related/GlobalFindexDatabase2025.csv>
- The published file is 8,577 rows by 438 columns, covering six survey years and
  every breakdown. `00_download_sources.R` filters it to 2024, the gender
  breakdown and the internet question, and converts proportions to percentages.
- Gives me: `internet_women`, `internet_men`

## Source 2 — Economic and education outcomes

**World Bank World Development Indicators**, retrieved through the `WDI` R
package, which queries the World Bank API by indicator code rather than
downloading a file. For each country I take the most recent value between 2021
and 2024, and keep a column recording which year it came from.

- Landing page: <https://databank.worldbank.org/source/world-development-indicators>
- R package: <https://cran.r-project.org/package=WDI>

| Indicator code | What it measures | My column |
|---|---|---|
| `NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD` | GDP per capita, PPP, constant international dollars | `gdp_pc_ppp` |
| `SL.TLF.CACT.FE.ZS` | Labour force participation rate, female, % of female population 15+ | `flfp` |
| `SE.SEC.ENRR.FE` | School enrollment, secondary, female, % gross | `sec_enroll_fem_gross` |
| `IT.NET.USER.ZS` | Individuals using the internet, % of population | `internet_total` |
| `SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS` | Urban population, % of total | `urban_pct` |
| `SP.POP.TOTL` | Used only to pull the region and income classification | — |

## Source 3 — Gender Inequality Index

**UNDP Human Development Report 2025**, composite indices complete time series.
The GII combines maternal mortality, adolescent births, parliamentary seats,
education and labour force participation into one score from 0 to 1, where
higher means more unequal. I use the 2023 value as a control.

- Landing page: <https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads>
- File used: <https://hdr.undp.org/sites/default/files/2025_HDR/HDR25_Composite_indices_complete_time_series.csv>
- Gives me: `gender_inequality_index`

## Which countries count as developing

The sample is defined by the **World Bank income classification** - low,
lower-middle and upper-middle income - with aggregate rows such as "World" and
"Sub-Saharan Africa" excluded. This is pulled in `00_download_sources.R`
alongside the indicators above, so the sample definition lives in code rather
than being chosen by hand.

**One measurement caveat worth stating up front.** `internet_total` comes from
the World Bank, while `internet_women` and `internet_men` come from Global
Findex. They are different surveys with different instruments and slightly
different definitions of an internet user. I use the World Bank figure as my
control for overall connectivity, which means it is not exactly the average of
my two gendered figures. I return to this in the limitations.



# Part 2: Summary statistics

```{r summary-table}
summary_table <- data %>%
  select(internet_women, internet_men, gap_diff, gap_ratio,
         gdp_pc_ppp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross,
         internet_total, urban_pct, gender_inequality_index) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    n       = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    mean    = round(mean(value,   na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd      = round(sd(value,     na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    min     = round(min(value,    na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median  = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    max     = round(max(value,    na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c(
    "internet_women", "internet_men", "gap_diff", "gap_ratio",
    "gdp_pc_ppp", "flfp", "sec_enroll_fem_gross",
    "internet_total", "urban_pct", "gender_inequality_index"))) %>%
  arrange(variable)

knitr::kable(summary_table)
```

**What to notice in the output.** The gap runs from −8.04 to +43.61 with a median
of 4.79 and a mean of 6.06. Mean above median is the arithmetic signature of a
right tail — a few very large values pulling the average up. `gap_ratio` passing
1.0 marks the countries where women are ahead.


# Part 3: What is missing

**What this does.** `across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))` counts missing values
in every column at once, then `pivot_longer` turns that one wide row into a
readable list and `filter(missing > 0)` drops the columns that are complete.

```{r missing-count}
data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") %>%
  filter(missing > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing))
```

**Counts are not enough.** Knowing that 15 countries lack an enrollment figure
tells me the size of the problem; knowing *which* countries tells me whether it
is likely to bias anything. So I name them.

```{r missing-who}
data %>%
  select(country, gdp_pc_ppp, sec_enroll_fem_gross, gender_inequality_index) %>%
  pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(is.na(value)) %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(n_missing = n(),
            countries = paste(sort(country), collapse = ", "),
            .groups = "drop")
```

Three things to say about this:

- Female secondary enrollment is my weakest variable. 15 of 89 countries have
  no figure, which drops my enrollment models to n = 74.
- The missingness is not random. The countries without an enrollment figure
  are mostly lower-income, which means the enrollment results describe a
  slightly better-off subset of my sample.
- I did not impute anything. Every model simply uses the countries that have
  the variables it needs, and I report the n for each one.

Region is **descriptive only**. It appears in two plots below and in none of my
models, so no coefficient anywhere in this project is adjusted for region.


## Visual 1: How big is the gap?

**The question:** how wide is the internet gender gap, and how much do
countries differ?

```{r fig-gap-hist, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = gap_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Most countries have a gap, but a few are extreme",
       subtitle = "Positive values mean men are further online than women",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       y = "Number of countries") +
  theme_minimal()

fig1
```

Twenty-one of 89 countries sit left of the line. The tallest bar is just above
zero, so the single most common situation is a near-equal gap. The right tail is
long and thin: 30 countries above 10 points, only five above 20, and then nothing
at all between 25 and 41 before Pakistan at 43.61, alone.

*The number of bins is a judgement call. Twenty shows the right tail without
breaking the distribution into noise.*


## Visual 2: Which countries are at the extremes?

**The question:** where is the gap widest, and where are women actually ahead?

A histogram can't carry names, so this is where they go.

```{r fig-extremes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
extremes <- bind_rows(
  data %>% slice_max(gap_diff, n = 10),
  data %>% slice_min(gap_diff, n = 5)
) %>%
  mutate(side = if_else(gap_diff > 0, "Men ahead", "Women ahead"))

fig2 <- ggplot(extremes, aes(x = reorder(country, gap_diff), y = gap_diff,
                             fill = side)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Men ahead" = "steelblue",
                               "Women ahead" = "darkorange")) +
  labs(title = "The ten widest gaps, and the five where women lead",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

fig2
```


## Visual 3: Is the gap worse where fewer people are online?

**The question:** does the gap shrink as a country gets more connected
overall? This matters because it is the reason I control for total internet
use later.

```{r fig-45, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5}
fig3 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = internet_men, y = internet_women)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.85, size = 2) +
  # Dark2 is colour-blind friendly, unlike ggplot's default palette
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Women's internet use against men's",
       subtitle = "Dashed line is equality. Below it, men are further online.",
       x = "Men online (%)", y = "Women online (%)", colour = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

fig3
```

The points sit tight to the line in the top right and fan out below it toward
the bottom left. The gap is widest exactly where overall connectivity is lowest.
**This is the visual justification for controlling for `internet_total`** — a
picture of a confound, which is easier to show than to describe.

## Visual 4: Where is the gap concentrated?

**The question:** is the gap a regional phenomenon or spread evenly?


```{r fig-region, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5}
fig4 <- data %>%
  mutate(region = fct_reorder(region, gap_diff, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = gap_diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "The gap by world region",
       subtitle = "Boxes show the middle half of countries; points are countries",
       x = NULL, y = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

fig4
```

Median gaps: South Asia 15.2, Sub-Saharan Africa 11.3, Latin America 1.7, Middle
East and North Africa 1.2, Europe and Central Asia 1.1, and East Asia and Pacific
−1.4, where women are ahead on average. Every region has countries on both sides
of zero, so this is a broad pattern with regional concentration rather than a
South Asia story in disguise.

I plot every country as a point as well as the box because with only five South
Asian countries a boxplot alone would overstate how solid that median is.

## Visual 5: The gap against each outcome

**The question:** before any controls, does the gap look related to my three
outcomes?


```{r fig-outcomes, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.6}
outcome_long <- data %>%
  select(country, gap_diff, log_gdp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(log_gdp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross),
               names_to = "outcome", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(outcome = recode(outcome,
    log_gdp              = "Logged GDP per capita",
    flfp                 = "Female labour force participation (%)",
    sec_enroll_fem_gross = "Female secondary enrollment (%)"))

fig5 <- ggplot(outcome_long, aes(x = gap_diff, y = value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Two slopes, and one flat line",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

fig5
```

This is the puzzle the analysis file solves. GDP and enrollment slope down.
Female labour force participation is flat.

Each panel's line is the bivariate model from `02_analysis.Rmd`: −0.039 for
logged GDP, −0.094 for participation, −1.207 for enrollment.



## Visual 6: The final figure

**The question:** what does the relationship between the gap and female labour
force participation look like among countries that are alike on overall internet
use and urbanisation?

A plain scatter of the two shows nothing, because two opposing effects cancel.
The added variable plot removes the part of each variable that the controls
already explain and shows what is left — which is the relationship the
regression actually estimates.

**How to read the code.** `lm(flfp ~ internet_total + urban_pct)` predicts
participation from the controls alone. `residuals()` returns what that prediction
missed, how far above or below each country sits relative to where its
connectivity and urbanisation alone would put it. The second line does the same
to the gap. Plotting one against the other compares countries that have been put
on a level footing. Everything after that is an ordinary scatter plot.

```{r fig-final, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.4}
# none of these four columns has a missing value, so the residuals line up
# with all 89 rows of the data frame
plot_data <- data
plot_data$flfp_resid <- residuals(lm(flfp ~ internet_total + urban_pct,
                                     data = data))
plot_data$gap_resid  <- residuals(lm(gap_diff ~ internet_total + urban_pct,
                                     data = data))

panel_raw <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(gap_diff, flfp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey45") +
  labs(title = "All 89 countries, unadjusted",
       subtitle = "No visible relationship (r = -0.05)",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       y = "Female labour force participation (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

panel_adj <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(gap_resid, flfp_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Among countries at similar internet use and urbanisation",
       subtitle = "-0.65 points of participation per point of gap (p = 0.004)",
       x = "Internet gender gap (residual)",
       y = "Female participation (residual)") +
  theme_minimal()

fig6 <- panel_raw + panel_adj
fig6
```

Nothing is literally held constant here. All 89 countries keep their own
internet penetration and their own urban share. What the code does is **remove**
the part of each variable that the controls can predict, leaving residuals that
are uncorrelated with internet use and urbanisation by construction. That is why
the panel is titled as a comparison between similar countries rather than as
something being fixed at a value.

There are pairs in my own data where this comparison can be seen directly. Iraq
and Paraguay differ by 0.1 of a percentage point in overall internet use and by
0.03 in urban share — effectively identical on both controls — but their gaps are
23 points apart, and Iraq's female participation is far lower. Such matched pairs
are rare, which is exactly why the comparison has to be made by a regression
across all 89 countries rather than by eye.

## Checking that the figure is the model

```{r line-check}
m_bivariate <- lm(flfp ~ gap_diff, data = data)
m_full      <- lm(flfp ~ gap_diff + internet_total + urban_pct, data = data)

flfp_r <- residuals(lm(flfp     ~ internet_total + urban_pct, data = data))
gap_r  <- residuals(lm(gap_diff ~ internet_total + urban_pct, data = data))
m_av   <- lm(flfp_r ~ gap_r)

tibble(
  panel           = c("Left: unadjusted", "Right: adjusted"),
  slope_in_figure = c(coef(m_bivariate)["gap_diff"], coef(m_av)["gap_r"]),
  coef_in_model   = c(coef(m_bivariate)["gap_diff"], coef(m_full)["gap_diff"])
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 5)))

# exactly equal, not approximately
all.equal(unname(coef(m_full)["gap_diff"]), unname(coef(m_av)["gap_r"]))
```

```{r save-figs}

ggsave("figures/fig1_gap_distribution.png", fig1, width = 7,  height = 4,   dpi = 300)

ggsave("figures/fig4_by_region.png",        fig4, width = 7.5,height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig5_gap_vs_outcomes.png",  fig5, width = 9,  height = 3.6, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig6_final.png",            fig6, width = 10, height = 4.4, dpi = 300)

list.files("figures")
```

```{r save-table}
if (!dir.exists("results")) dir.create("results")
write_csv(summary_table, "results/summary_statistics.csv")
```
